content_voiceover: This slide repeats the same trio of exam questions on bypassing agents and inhibitor management, so let's reinforce the key facts. Activated prothrombin complex concentrate, or aPCC, marketed as FEIBA, is an established bypassing treatment for hemophilia patients with inhibitors, and the exam tests which factor it lacks, the answer is factor eight, since aPCC instead contains factors two, seven, nine, and ten, allowing it to bypass the missing factor eight step entirely. Next is a vignette about a three year old with severe hemophilia A who develops an inhibitor at a titer of 10.5 Bethesda units and starts immune tolerance induction. To declare success and safely discontinue ITI, three criteria must all be satisfied together, a persistently negative inhibitor titer under zero point six Bethesda units, factor eight recovery greater than sixty six percent of expected, and a factor eight half life of at least six hours. Watch for the classic distractor that flips the recovery threshold to less than or equal to sixty six percent, which is incorrect. Finally, the slide reviews the engineering strategies behind extended half life recombinant factor products used for hemophilia prophylaxis, fusion with the Fc portion of immunoglobulin, PEGylation, single chain factor eight engineered to bind von Willebrand factor, and albumin fusion are all legitimate, currently used approaches.
keypoints: aPCC (FEIBA) contains factors II, VII, IX, and X, but not factor VIII
Successful ITI requires inhibitor titer under 0.6 BU, FVIII recovery over 66%, and half-life at least 6 hours
Extended half-life technologies: Fc fusion, PEGylation, VWF-binding single-chain FVIII, and albumin fusion
keypoint_voiceover: Reinforcing the same three facts. aPCC bypasses factor eight because it deliberately excludes it, relying on factors two, seven, nine, and ten instead. Stopping immune tolerance induction requires all three criteria at once, low inhibitor titer, recovery above sixty six percent, and a half-life of six hours or longer. And extended half-life products extend circulation time through Fc fusion, PEGylation, VWF-binding engineering, or albumin fusion.
